title: Kama burned to ash, and not gone
hook: Shiva burns the god of love to ash, yet love stays one of life's rightful aims.
carry: kama is a rightful aim, in its fitting place
tomorrow: a powerful man wants what isn't his. which aim should have won?

segments.voice: Yesterday closed dharma, artha, kama: let none swallow the rest: your own dharma differs, the dharma for all doesn't. Today, a new book, and the god who shares its name.

The gods need Shiva to marry Parvati, but Shiva sits deep in meditation, wanting nothing. So they send Kama, the god of love, with his bow of sugarcane and his arrows of flowers. Spring arrives out of season. Kama takes aim at the yogi. Shiva's third eye opens, and fire turns Kama to ash. His wife Rati weeps over the ashes. Yet love doesn't leave the world. In the tellings Kama lives on without a body, as Ananga, the bodiless one, and Parvati wins Shiva in the end by her own devotion and discipline.
screen: `A FLOWER ARROW AT A YOGI.` → `THE THIRD EYE OPENS.` → `ASH, BUT LOVE REMAINS.`

segments.voice: Hindu teaching doesn't do what Shiva's fire seems to do. It doesn't abolish desire. It names kama, joy and love, as one of the aims of a human life, beside dharma, artha and moksha. The Kama Sutra is famous for one thing, and its frank chapters for adults stay on the shelf here. But it opens with a chapter that reads like philosophy. Vatsyayana, the author it names, defines each aim. Dharma is doing what scripture asks and holding back from what it forbids. Artha is gaining what's worth having, learning, land, goods, and friends, then protecting it and helping it grow. And kama is the enjoyment of fitting things by the five senses, with the mind and the self taking part. Two words carry the weight. Fitting: pleasure that suits, not just any appetite; many readers add, suited to the moment too. One way to read Kama's ash with this chapter in hand: his arrow flew at the wrong moment, at a yogi deep in meditation. And the mind and the self: pleasure with someone actually there for it. Earlier on this path, the Gita called kama a smoke that clouds what we know. Here the same word names a rightful aim, with limits. The tradition holds both.
screen: `DESIRE NAMED, NOT ABOLISHED.` · `VATSYAYANA DEFINES EACH AIM.` · `FITTING JOY OF THE FIVE SENSES.` · `WITH THE MIND AND SELF THERE.` · then, large: `A RIGHTFUL AIM, IN ITS FITTING PLACE.`

segments.voice: If there's something near you with a smell, tea, soap, an orange peel, bring it close and breathe it in slowly. Stay with that one smell for the whole sit, your whole attention there. If you pray, end with a quiet thank you, the way many Hindus offer food before they eat. If you don't, simply notice it fully.
The Kama Sutra's ethics chapter: where kama is defined as fitting joy of the five senses, with the mind and the self there too.
screen: `THE KAMA SUTRA'S ETHICS CHAPTER — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: kama is a rightful aim, in its fitting place. Shiva's fire didn't end love. Until tomorrow.

howItsDone: Kama, the god of love, is pictured with a sugarcane bow and flower arrows; his burning by Shiva is told in the Puranas and in Kalidasa's poem Kumarasambhava. Scholars of Hindu ethics read the Kama Sutra's opening chapters beside the dharma texts, because they define dharma, artha and kama.

kama.meaning: pleasure and love; one of the three aims of life

Audience: the hook names the book's reputation and says the rest stays on the shelf; nothing beyond the ethics chapter is described. A parent-safe framing; confirm.

Confirm in KS 1.2: dharma as obedience to the shastra's commands and prohibitions, learned from shruti and those versed in it; artha as acquiring vidya, land, gold, cattle, grain, goods and friends and protecting and increasing them, learned from officials and experts in trade; kama as enjoyment of appropriate objects by the five senses assisted by mind and self (atman). Paraphrased; no Burton/Arbuthnot (1883) wording quoted (not on the validator's list).
Gita 3.37–3.39 (kama as enemy, smoke over fire) points back to an earlier day of the path; the framing 'one long conversation about desire' is interpretive.
